summary:
Mayotte stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as in France proper.

No law criminalises being trans or being in a same-sex relationship. Same-sex marriage has been available on the island since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975, and the National Assembly's vote simplifying legal gender change for trans people extends to the department.

Placement in custody follows the gender marker carried on the identity document under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code. Trans women are therefore typically held in all-male facilities, where other detainees threaten them; anatomy does not determine where a person is placed.

The national detention-places watchdog CGLPL reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty. Its opinion rests on referrals received since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people, and on inspections at which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse. Those findings bind Mayotte's establishments as French establishments.

Formal rights and lived experience diverge. A 2023 account of Bruno Agar, a teacher at the university centre of Mayotte, and his Malagasy partner describes a long and complicated path before the two married at Sada Town Hall, on a predominantly Muslim island where same-sex marriage remains a rarity in Africa and the Islamic world.

Legal representation on the island is thin. A gay-friendly lawyer directory returns no referenced practitioner for Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi, Sada and other towns, while Maître Isabelle Zribi, a lawyer at the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation based in Paris, is listed as available to take instructions.
tangentialFactors:
Mayotte carries the fullest set of formal protections of any jurisdiction in this part of the world: marriage equality, gender-identity anti-discrimination coverage and a simplified route to legal gender change all sit in the same framework, none of them local inventions but extensions of French law.

The prison findings are national rather than local. The CGLPL opinion concerns French places of deprivation of liberty as a class, drawn from referrals and inspections conducted in metropolitan establishments, and it says nothing specific about how a trans detainee would be held in Mayotte. The same is true of Article D248: the rule is French, its application here is by extension.

The documented friction is social rather than statutory. The 2023 account of a binational same-sex couple shows a marriage that was legally available yet procedurally drawn out, on an island where the surrounding legal and cultural environment offers no comparable recognition.

Evidence of local support infrastructure is limited to a single directory listing, which is a weak instrument: absence of a referenced lawyer there does not establish that no practitioner on the island would accept such a case.
localsOnly:
Residents may use the simplified civil-status procedure for legal gender change adopted by the National Assembly, on the same terms as residents of metropolitan departments.

Residents held in custody are placed according to the gender marker on their identity document, which for trans women generally means all-male facilities and the exposure to threats that the CGLPL documented across the French prison system.

Residents seeking counsel on LGBT or family matters find no referenced practitioner in Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi, Sada or the other towns covered by the directory; metropolitan counsel, including Maître Isabelle Zribi admitted to the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, are the listed option.

Marriage between two men or two women is available at Mayotte's town halls, as at Sada Town Hall, and the anti-discrimination statute covering gender identity applies to employment and services on the island.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory reports a trans person detained in Mayotte, the facility used, or any incident involving one; the prison material describes the French framework and metropolitan inspections, and its application to local establishments is an extension of law rather than a documented local case.

Whether the CGLPL's 2021 findings have been acted on in Mayotte, and whether any complaint by a trans detainee here has produced a remedy, is unresolved and not sourced.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare on the island, and whether the simplified gender-change procedure has in fact been completed by any resident, are not sourced.

The enforcement of the gender-identity anti-discrimination provisions locally, including any recorded complaint or hate-crime incident with an outcome, is not sourced.

The lawyer directory's coverage is self-described as incomplete, so the absence of a listed practitioner should be read as an absence of reference rather than a finding that none exists.
